ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.name: Snakehead fish braised with green bananas
aliases: Snakehead fish braised with green plantain
ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.serving_basis: One family pot of braised snakehead fish and green bananas for four people.
ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.description: Snakehead fish is marinated with fish sauce, pepper and chili, then braised with green bananas until both absorb a light caramel glaze. Bếp Việt adapts the method for a home kitchen, keeping the bananas tender but intact and the sauce gently reduced.
ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.finished_dish: Firm, tender fish pieces nestled among golden-brown green banana chunks in a glossy, savory-sweet braising sauce.
ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.serving: Arrange the fish and bananas in a shallow dish, spoon over a little sauce and serve hot with steamed rice and boiled vegetables.
tips: Soak cut green bananas in salted lemon water to slow discoloration.
Marinate the fish for about 30 minutes and sear it briefly before adding liquid.
Braise over low heat, add hot water as needed and avoid vigorous stirring.

ca-loc-kho-chuoi-xanh.time_note: About 90 minutes, including 30 minutes of marinating.

preparation_steps: Rinse and cut the fish into steaks. Rub lightly with salt and vinegar, rinse again and pat dry.
Lightly peel and cut the bananas; soak them in salted water with lime juice.
Mince garlic, slice shallots and chili. Marinate the fish with fish sauce, pepper, chili sauce, sugar, garlic and chili for 30 minutes.
cooking_steps: Caramelize part of the sugar with a little water until amber, then add oil and fry the shallots until fragrant.
Sear both sides of the fish until firm. Add the bananas and remaining marinade, turning gently to coat.
Pour in hot water to nearly cover the fish. Bring to a gentle boil, cover and braise on low heat for 25–30 minutes, until the bananas are tender and the sauce has reduced.

bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.name: Hanoi snail and green banana noodle soup
aliases: Snails cooked with banana and beans and eaten with noodles
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.serving_basis: Four bowls of snail noodle soup with green banana, tofu, pork belly and herbs.
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.description: Banana and bean snail vermicelli evokes the rich taste of green bananas, crunchy snails, yellow tofu and mildly sour broth from the batch. Vietnamese Kitchen prepares enough broth for the family, cooks the bananas until soft but keeps the pieces and adds the snails later so they don't get tough.
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.finished_dish: A hot bowl of rice vermicelli with tender snails, soft nutty green banana, seasoned tofu and a golden broth fragrant with fermented rice and perilla.
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.serving: Blanch the vermicelli and divide among bowls. Add the broth, snails, banana, tofu and pork, then garnish with perilla, lolot leaves and scallions. Serve hot.
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.image_alt: A bowl of Hanoi snail and green banana noodle soup with snails, green banana, fried tofu and perilla in a lightly golden broth.
bun-oc-chuoi-dau-ha-noi.time_note: Soaking time for snails depends on type and source; Snails need to be completely cooked before eating.
tips: Soak live snails in clean water with a few chili slices or rice-rinsing water, rinse thoroughly, then boil completely before removing the meat.
Soak the green banana in salted water with a little vinegar to reduce browning and astringency.
Stir-fry the snails separately and return them to the pot only for the last few minutes to keep them tender-crisp.

preparation_steps: If using live snails, soak them for 1–2 hours in clean water with a few chili slices or rice-rinsing water, changing the water once; rinse several times.
Boil the snails until fully cooked, remove the meat and discard inedible parts; drain. Cut and soak the green banana in salted vinegar water, then prepare the tomatoes, herbs and pork.
Fry the tofu until evenly golden. Sauté some shallot with turmeric, quickly stir-fry the snails with a little fish sauce, then set aside.
cooking_steps: Sauté the remaining shallots and garlic, add the pork belly and cook until firm. Add the tomatoes and green banana and toss with the turmeric.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and skim. Mix the fermented rice starter and shrimp paste with a little water, strain into the pot, season with fish sauce and simmer the banana for 15–20 minutes.
Add the tofu and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in the cooked snails for the final 2–3 minutes, adjust the sour and savory balance, then turn off the heat.
Blanch the vermicelli and divide among bowls. Top with snails, banana, tofu and pork, ladle over the broth, garnish with perilla, lolot leaves and scallions, and serve hot.

banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.name: Phung Cong steamed rice cakes
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.serving_basis: Twelve tapered rice cakes filled with pork and wood ear mushrooms, three per person.
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.description: Phung Cong harrow wheel has an elongated shape like a harrow tooth, a layer of soft rice flour hugs the meat, onions and fragrant wood ear mushrooms. Viet Kitchen compiled a recipe using pre-ground rice flour, stirring the flour until smooth, then wrapping it in banana leaves and steaming.
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.finished_dish: A neat tapered cake with soft, chewy rice dough, well-seasoned pork, lightly crunchy wood ear mushrooms and a subtle banana-leaf aroma.
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.serving: Unwrap while warm and enjoy as is or with lightly seasoned fish sauce. These cakes are best freshly steamed.
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.image_alt: Phung Cong rice cakes wrapped in banana leaves, with one unwrapped to reveal the soft rice dough and pork and wood ear filling.
banh-rang-bua-phung-cong.time_note: The dough needs to rest before stirring; Steam until the dough layer is evenly transparent from the center to the edges.
tips: Stir the batter constantly over low heat until it is partially cooked, smooth and free of lumps.
Spread the dough evenly, place the filling in the center and seal both ends so the cake does not split during steaming.
Steam until the rice dough turns translucent and chewy; do not crowd the steamer.

preparation_steps: Mix the rice flour with water and half the salt until smooth; let rest for 30 minutes. Soak, rinse and finely chop the wood ear mushrooms.
Combine the pork with wood ear mushrooms, shallots, fish sauce, pepper and the remaining salt. Heat the oil and stir-fry until just cooked; let cool.
Blanch the banana leaves until pliable, pat dry and cut into pieces large enough to wrap the tapered cakes.
cooking_steps: Set the batter over low heat and stir constantly until thick, smooth and resistant; remove from the heat and mix in a little oil.

Spoon the batter onto a banana leaf and spread it into a long strip. Add filling down the center and cover with batter. Roll into a tapered plough-tooth shape, fold the ends and tie with bamboo strips.
Arrange the cakes in a steamer over boiling water and steam for 20–25 minutes, until the rice dough is translucent and chewy. Rest for a few minutes and serve warm.

nem-buoi-tay-ninh.name: Tay Ninh pomelo peel vegetarian rolls
aliases: Vegetarian spring rolls with grapefruit peel
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.serving_basis: Twelve small vegetarian pomelo-peel rolls, served with aromatic leaves and pepper salt.
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.description: Tay Ninh grapefruit spring rolls use grapefruit pulp and green papaya to create vegetarian spring rolls with a crunchy texture, mild sour taste and roasted smell. Vietnamese Kitchen compiles small batches, thoroughly removes bitterness, seasoning with vegetable spices and instructions for short fermentation in clean utensils.
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.finished_dish: Rosy-orange vegetarian rolls with a light crunch from pomelo pith and papaya, fragrant toasted rice powder and a gentle tang with a hint of chili.
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.serving: Unwrap and serve the rolls with Vietnamese coriander or young erythrina leaves and pepper salt. Refrigerate once they reach the desired tang.
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.image_alt: Plant-based Tay Ninh pomelo-peel rolls in a rosy orange hue, dusted with toasted rice powder and served with green leaves, pepper and chili.
nem-buoi-tay-ninh.time_note: Fermentation time depends on temperature and degree of drying of ingredients; Keep cold until the spring rolls are just sour and tender.
tips: Boil and rinse the pomelo pith several times to reduce bitterness, then squeeze very dry.
Use clean utensils, dry wrapping leaves and fresh ingredients. Do not eat if the rolls smell unusual, feel slimy or show signs of spoilage.
Fermentation time varies with room temperature. Check after a few hours and refrigerate as soon as the rolls become mildly tangy.

preparation_steps: Remove the green outer peel and slice the pomelo pith very thinly. Soak in salted water for 10 minutes, rinse and briefly boil; repeat if still bitter, then squeeze dry.
Shred the green papaya, rinse briefly and drain; gently squeeze out excess water. Mince the garlic and chili and crush the peppercorns.
Toast rice for the toasted rice powder if needed. Wash and thoroughly dry the erythrina and banana leaves; prepare a clean mixing surface.
cooking_steps: Mix the pomelo pith and papaya with sugar, salt, garlic, chili, pepper, annatto oil and toasted rice powder; gently knead until the mixture holds together.
Shape into 12 small balls, wrap each in an erythrina leaf, then in banana leaf. Place in a clean covered container.
Ferment briefly in a cool, airy place, checking after 3–5 hours. Once mildly tangy, refrigerate and serve with Vietnamese coriander.

banh-pia-soc-trang.name: Soc Trang pia pastries
banh-pia-soc-trang.serving_basis: Eight medium pia pastries filled with mung bean and durian, each with a salted egg yolk.
banh-pia-soc-trang.description: Soc Trang pia cake stands out with its multi-layered crust and durian green bean filling, often with salted egg yolk in the middle. Vietnamese Kitchen prepares a batch of family cakes using the technique of water dough coating oil dough, rolling it many times to create a fragrant spongy crust.
banh-pia-soc-trang.finished_dish: A fragrant golden pastry with delicate flaky layers and a rich mung bean and durian filling wrapped around a gently salty egg yolk.
banh-pia-soc-trang.serving: Let the pastries cool completely and serve with hot tea. Store in an airtight container and observe a safe shelf life because the filling contains egg and moisture.
banh-pia-soc-trang.image_alt: Golden, flaky Soc Trang pia pastries, one cut open to show its mung bean and durian filling with a salted egg yolk.
banh-pia-soc-trang.time_note: It is necessary to let the dough rest and roll it several times; Baking time depends on the oven and cake size.
tips: Rest the dough between rolling stages so the layers do not shrink and are easier to coil.
Cook the filling until firm enough to roll into balls; a wet filling will prevent the pastry from separating into layers.
Bake in two stages and brush with egg yolk during the second stage for an even golden finish without burning.

preparation_steps: Soak the mung beans, steam until tender and mash smooth. Cook with sugar, some of the rendered pork fat and durian until cohesive; add toasted glutinous rice flour if still wet.
Divide the filling into eight portions and wrap each around a salted egg yolk. Cool and keep chilled while preparing the dough.
Knead the water dough with some of the flour, sugar, salt, water and a little fat until smooth. Mix the remaining flour with fat to make the shortening dough; rest both for 20 minutes.
cooking_steps: Divide the water dough into eight portions and wrap each around a portion of shortening dough. Roll out, coil, turn lengthwise and roll once more to create layers.
Enclose each filling ball in a dough portion, seal the edges and place seam-side down on a lined baking tray.
Bake at 190°C for about 18 minutes until the pastry begins to set. Remove, brush with egg yolk, add sesame if desired and bake another 12–15 minutes until golden.
Cool the pastries completely on a rack before storing in an airtight container or serving with hot tea.
